idiom_name: std::expected<T, E> with and_then / transform / or_else
implementation_notes: C++23 ships std::expected<T, E>: it holds either the expected value of type T or an unexpected value of type E, is never valueless, and provides the error-contract surface directly - the observers has_value/operator bool, value, error, value_or and error_or, and the monadic operations and_then (chain a further step returning an expected), transform and transform_error (map one side) and or_else (recover). That is the C++ spelling of the short-circuiting railway, and it replaces the hand-written enum-plus-union result entirely. The unchecked accessors value() and operator* are the unwrap trap - they throw or are undefined on the wrong alternative - so ordinary code uses value_or/and_then. The pattern still needs a deliberate error type E and one conversion at the boundary where exceptions or errno arrive.
pitfalls: value()/operator* on the wrong alternative is the unwrap trap: it throws bad_expected_access (or is undefined in unchecked builds); keep value_or/and_then for production paths.
and_then requires the callable to return an expected of the same error type E; a differently typed error has to be folded in with transform_error first or the chain will not compile.
The error is stored inline, not boxed: a large or throwing E inflates the return value and every move/copy of the expected.

variants.name: tl::expected single-header library (pre-C++23)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++23 the same contract comes from single-header ports: tl::expected follows the p0323 interface and adds the chaining helpers - map and map_error for one-sided transformations, and_then for steps that themselves return an expected, and or_else for recovery - so a whole sequence reads as a call pipeline instead of repeating if (!r) return r; checks, as the library's own before/after example shows. Choose it while the toolchain cannot move to C++23; the error type, the unwrap discipline and the boundary conversion are unchanged, and migrating later is mostly a type-name change. Its assertions on wrong-alternative access can be compiled out, so the discipline still comes from the code and review, not the library.
variants.idiom_name: tl::expected<T, E> with map / and_then / or_else
pitfalls: The header is a pinned dependency to vendor; without it the local build and the CI compiler matrix diverge silently.
Accessing the wrong alternative only trips TL_ASSERT (assert by default), which release builds compile out - the same trap as value().
